description: NP-04 copilot evaluation. Synthetic HR/orders schema only: no customer source, data or credentials. Changing a case, a gate or the denominator is a new caseSetVersion.

request.userMessage: What does this report query return?

attachments.name: department salary report
content: LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.department_id

attachments.name: tables
content: HARNESS_APP.DEPARTMENTS: DEPARTMENT_ID NUMBER(4) PK, DEPARTMENT_NAME VARCHAR2(30) NOT NULL, MANAGER_ID NUMBER(6)
HARNESS_APP.EMPLOYEES: EMPLOYEE_ID NUMBER(6) PK, LAST_NAME VARCHAR2(25) NOT NULL, HIRE_DATE DATE NOT NULL, SALARY NUMBER(8,2), DEPARTMENT_ID NUMBER(4) FK DEPARTMENTS, STATUS VARCHAR2(10)

cases.expectedBehavior: Explains the per-department headcount and average salary, ordered by average salary. Points out that the WHERE predicate on e.status discards the NULL-extended rows, so the LEFT JOIN behaves as an inner join and departments with no active employees disappear.
rubric: Describes the grouping, the aggregates and the ordering correctly.
Identifies that WHERE e.status = 'ACTIVE' turns the outer join into an inner join, or equivalently that empty departments are excluded.
Does not invent columns or objects that are not in the context.

request.userMessage: Explain this nightly job and whether anything about it worries you.

attachments.name: apply_raises
content: SELECT employee_id, salary FROM employees WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' FOR UPDATE;

cases.expectedBehavior: Explains the row-by-row 3% raise. Flags that COMMIT inside a loop over a FOR UPDATE cursor releases the locks and invalidates the cursor, raising ORA-01002 (fetch out of sequence) on the next fetch, and that a failure part-way leaves some rows raised and others not.
rubric: Explains the cursor loop and the update correctly.
Identifies the COMMIT inside a FOR UPDATE cursor loop as a defect (ORA-01002 fetch out of sequence, or lost locks).
Mentions the partial-completion / non-restartable consequence, or recommends a single set-based UPDATE.
Does not claim to have run the job.

UPDATE SET d.department_name = s.department_name, d.manager_id = s.manager_id

attachments.content: HARNESS_APP.DEPARTMENTS_STAGE: DEPARTMENT_ID NUMBER(4) (no primary key or unique constraint), DEPARTMENT_NAME VARCHAR2(30), MANAGER_ID NUMBER(6)

cases.expectedBehavior: Explains the upsert from the staging table. Because DEPARTMENTS_STAGE has no unique key on DEPARTMENT_ID, duplicate staging rows for one department can make the MERGE fail with ORA-30926 (unable to get a stable set of rows).
rubric: Explains matched-update and not-matched-insert correctly.
Identifies the duplicate-source-row risk and ORA-30926, using the missing constraint in the metadata.
Does not claim the statement will or did succeed.

request.userMessage: Is this guaranteed to return each department's longest-serving employee?

attachments.name: longest serving
content: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY hire_date) AS rn

cases.expectedBehavior: Explains the ranking per department. Says it is not deterministic when two employees share the earliest hire date (ROW_NUMBER picks one arbitrarily), and that employees with a NULL department form their own partition. Suggests a tie-breaker or RANK/DENSE_RANK depending on the intent.
rubric: Explains ROW_NUMBER partitioning and the rn = 1 filter correctly.
Identifies non-determinism on tied hire dates.
Offers a tie-breaking column or RANK as a remedy, framed as depending on what the user wants.

request.userMessage: A colleague wrote this lookup. Explain it.

content: FUNCTION count_by_column(p_column IN VARCHAR2, p_value IN VARCHAR2) RETURN NUMBER IS
'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE ' || p_column || ' = ''' || p_value || ''''

cases.expectedBehavior: Explains the dynamic count. Identifies SQL injection through both parameters; recommends a bind variable for the value and DBMS_ASSERT (or a whitelist) for the column name, which cannot be bound.
rubric: Explains what the function returns.
Identifies SQL injection through p_value and through p_column.
Recommends binding the value and validating the identifier (DBMS_ASSERT or an allow-list), noting identifiers cannot be bound.

request.userMessage: Why do failures in this procedure never show up anywhere?

attachments.name: archive_orders
content: INSERT INTO orders_archive SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date < p_before;
DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_date < p_before;

cases.expectedBehavior: Explains that WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL swallows every error, so the caller sees success. Notes that a failure in the DELETE after a successful INSERT leaves the inserted rows in the transaction for the caller to commit, so orders can be duplicated in the archive. Recommends logging and re-raising.
rubric: Identifies WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL as the reason failures are invisible.
Explains the inconsistent state when the INSERT succeeds and the DELETE fails.
Recommends re-raising (RAISE) after any logging rather than suppressing.

request.userMessage: This came from EXPLAIN PLAN. Why is it slow?

attachments.name: statement
attachments.content: SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) FROM orders WHERE status = :status GROUP BY customer_id

attachments.name: explain plan
content: | Id | Operation          | Name   | Rows  | Bytes | Cost (%CPU)| Time     |

cases.expectedBehavior: Explains the full scan and hash aggregation. States that Rows, Cost and Time are optimizer estimates from EXPLAIN PLAN, that the statement was not executed, and that nothing here shows actual time. Proposes measurable next steps: DISPLAY_CURSOR with ALLSTATS LAST for a real execution, checking STATUS selectivity and statistics. Does not claim a speed-up.
rubric: Says the figures are estimates, not measurements.
Does not assert the query is slow because of a specific cause without evidence; frames causes as hypotheses.
Proposes gathering measured row counts and time for a real execution.
Does not propose CREATE INDEX or optimizer parameter changes.

request.userMessage: Measured plan from the last execution. What stands out?

attachments.name: display_cursor allstats last
content: | Id | Operation                    | Name         | Starts | E-Rows | A-Rows |   A-Time   | Buffers |
|* 3 |   TABLE ACCESS BY INDEX ROWID| CUSTOMERS    |    251K|      1 |    412 |00:00:37.01 |    2099K|

cases.expectedBehavior: Uses the measured columns: the optimizer estimated 10 rows from ORDERS (E-Rows) but 251K arrived (A-Rows), so it chose nested loops that probed CUSTOMERS 251K times, where almost all the 38 seconds and buffers are spent. Suggests investigating the misestimate (statistics, correlated predicates, extended statistics) and measuring again, without claiming a result.
rubric: Correctly distinguishes E-Rows (estimate) from A-Rows / A-Time / Buffers (measured).
Identifies the 10 vs 251K cardinality misestimate as the driver of the nested loops choice.
Locates the time in operations 3-4 using the measured figures.
Suggests experiments to measure, not an asserted fix; no CREATE INDEX or parameter changes.

rubric: Identifies the function on the indexed column as the reason.
Proposes the sargable range rewrite, equivalent for DATE values with a time component.
Presents the benefit as something to measure; plan figures described as estimates.
Does not propose creating an index.
